report:
**Conclusion:** Your answer—“no”—best reflects the current overall evidence: probiotics should not be expected to reliably shorten acute infectious diarrhea. The evidence is inconsistent, highly dependent on the particular organism/strain and setting, and the most rigorous recent evidence does not show a clinically meaningful benefit.

A 2020 Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials found that the certainty of evidence was low to very low and concluded that probiotics probably make little or no difference to diarrhea lasting at least 48 hours; results for mean duration were too heterogeneous and bias-prone to establish a dependable effect. This overturned earlier, more favorable versions of the review.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea

Strong evidence *against* a routine benefit comes from two large, blinded North American pediatric trials: one (971 children) tested *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG and the other (886 children) tested a combined probiotic. Neither improved gastroenteritis outcomes versus placebo, including duration/severity measures.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597

**Why some still say “yes”:** older, smaller trials and meta-analyses—often in hospitalized children and using specific strains—reported modest shortening. Accordingly, the 2017 IDSA guideline says probiotics *may* be offered to immunocompetent adults and children, but this is only a **weak** recommendation with **moderate** evidence, not a recommendation for routine use.  
https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/infectious-diarrhea/

Oral rehydration remains the essential treatment. Avoid probiotics or obtain clinician advice if immunocompromised, critically ill, or with central venous access.
